questions.stem: A platform team's CLAUDE.md says "Always run Prettier on any file you change." Even so, about one in five pull requests produced with Claude Code fails the formatting check in CI, because Claude sometimes skips the step at the end of long sessions. The team wants formatting to happen after every single edit, with the most reliable result and minimal ongoing effort. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Move the Prettier rule to the top of CLAUDE.md and mark it IMPORTANT so it is less likely to be lost as the session grows.
Add several before-and-after examples of correctly formatted files to CLAUDE.md so Claude learns the expected style.
Add a PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write to the shared .claude/settings.json that runs Prettier on the changed file.
Create a format-code skill with a clear description so Claude invokes it automatically whenever it finishes editing a file.

questions.explanation: Anything that must happen **every time with zero exceptions** belongs in a hook, not in instructions. A `PostToolUse` hook with matcher `Edit|Write` runs deterministically after each file edit, and putting it in the committed `.claude/settings.json` applies it to the whole team. CLAUDE.md is advisory context; the docs describe hooks as deterministic and CLAUDE.md as advisory.

whyWrong.A: Emphasis can help a single rule stand out, but it is still probabilistic guidance. The failure rate drops; it does not reach zero.
whyWrong.B: Examples teach style, but the problem is that the formatting step is skipped, not that Claude misunderstands it. Examples also add context on every turn.
whyWrong.D: A skill is invoked when Claude (or a user) decides it is relevant, so it is still model-chosen and can be skipped, just like the CLAUDE.md rule.

questions.mindset: Must happen every time: use a hook. Should usually happen: use instructions.

questions.stem: A developer is about to build a per-tenant billing export with Claude Code. She knows the goal but has not worked out the edge cases, the failure handling, or how the export screen should behave. On the last feature like this, Claude produced a plausible implementation that missed several requirements nobody had written down, and the long session was hard to steer by the end. Which TWO practices from Claude Code's recommended workflow BEST fit this situation? Choose TWO.

options.text: Write one long prompt listing every requirement she can think of, then let Claude implement the feature without asking her anything further.
Do the requirements discussion and the implementation in the same session, so every nuance of the discussion stays in Claude's context.
Skip the requirements step and run the build in auto mode, so Claude can settle open design questions without stopping to ask.
Start with a short prompt and have Claude interview her with the AskUserQuestion tool about edge cases and tradeoffs, then write a spec file.
Once the spec is complete, start a fresh session to implement it, with the written spec as the reference instead of the earlier Q&A.

questions.explanation: For larger features the docs recommend letting **Claude interview you**: start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to use the `AskUserQuestion` tool to probe implementation details, UI, edge cases and tradeoffs, then write a complete spec (for example `SPEC.md`). The interview surfaces the requirements she has not thought of yet, which a list she writes herself cannot do. Then **start a fresh session** to implement: the new session has a clean context focused on implementation, and the written spec carries everything that matters from the Q&A.

whyWrong.A: A prompt can only contain what she already knows, and the problem is the requirements nobody has worked out yet. The interview exists to surface those.
whyWrong.B: The Q&A fills the context before any code is written, which repeats the hard-to-steer long session. The spec file already holds what matters, so a clean session is better.
whyWrong.C: Auto mode has a classifier review actions instead of prompting you about permissions. It does not settle product requirements, so Claude would still be guessing at them, just without asking.

questions.mindset: Surface unknown requirements first, capture them in a durable spec, then implement in a clean context.

questions.stem: A team pasted its 14-step release-notes procedure into the project CLAUDE.md. It is used once every two weeks by whoever is on release rotation. CLAUDE.md is now about 400 lines, and developers notice that Claude ignores some everyday coding rules in the same file. The team wants to keep the procedure shared through git and restore everyday rule-following with the smallest structural change. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Move the procedure into a project skill at .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md and delete it from CLAUDE.md.
Split the procedure into a separate markdown file and pull it back into CLAUDE.md with an @import so the main file stays short.
Move the procedure into each rotation member's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so it only loads for the people who need it.
Keep the procedure in CLAUDE.md but mark each everyday coding rule as IMPORTANT so those rules stand out from the procedure.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads in **every** session, so it should hold only broadly applicable rules. A bloated file causes Claude to lose important instructions. Occasional, task-specific workflows belong in a **skill**. Only its name and description sit in context until it is invoked, and a project skill under `.claude/skills/` is shared through git. For a workflow with side effects that should only run on request, `disable-model-invocation: true` keeps it manual and keeps it out of Claude's context until `/release-notes` is run.

whyWrong.B: `@import`s load at launch, so they organize the text but do not reduce context cost. The bloat remains.
whyWrong.C: User-level CLAUDE.md is personal and not version-controlled, which breaks the shared-through-git requirement. It also still loads in every session for those users.
whyWrong.D: When many lines are emphasized, none of them stands out. This also leaves the root cause, an oversized always-loaded file, in place.

questions.mindset: Always-relevant goes in CLAUDE.md; sometimes-relevant goes in a skill (progressive disclosure).

questions.stem: Before changing a large legacy monolith, a developer asks Claude Code to work out how token refresh flows through the authentication code. Claude reads several hundred files in the main session. By the time implementation starts, Claude is forgetting constraints the developer stated at the beginning. For the next task like this, which workflow change MOST effectively keeps implementation quality high?

options.text: Switch the session to a model with a larger context window so the exploration and the implementation both fit comfortably.
Ask Claude to read the files in smaller batches and write a summary of each batch into the main conversation as it goes.
Run /clear as soon as exploration finishes so the implementation phase starts with a clean, empty context window.
Delegate the investigation to a subagent such as the built-in Explore agent and have it report back only a concise summary.

questions.explanation: Context is the main constraint, and performance degrades as it fills. **Subagents run in their own context window** and report back only a summary, so the verbose file reads never enter the main conversation and the implementation context stays clean. This is the documented pattern: "use subagents to investigate X".

whyWrong.A: A bigger window delays the problem without fixing it. Irrelevant file contents still dilute attention, and every turn costs more.
whyWrong.B: All the reading still happens in the main context, so the per-batch summaries add to the load rather than removing it.
whyWrong.C: `/clear` throws away the findings along with the noise, so the implementation phase loses what exploration discovered.

questions.mindset: Isolate noisy discovery in a separate context and return only the distilled result.

questions.stem: A developer runs two Claude Code sessions in parallel in the same repository checkout: one builds a billing feature and the other refactors logging. The sessions keep overwriting each other's files and leaving the build broken for both. What is the simplest built-in way to let both sessions work in parallel without collisions?

options.text: Have the two sessions work on separate git branches in the same checkout, running git checkout before each prompt.
Start each session in its own isolated git worktree, for example with claude --worktree billing and claude --worktree logging.
Tell each session in its first prompt which directories belong to its feature and that it must not touch anything else.
Put both sessions in plan mode so that every edit has to be approved before Claude writes it to disk.

questions.explanation: `claude --worktree <name>` (`-w`) creates an isolated checkout under `.claude/worktrees/<name>/` at the repository root, on a new branch named `worktree-<name>`. Each session gets separate files while sharing the same git history and remote, which is the documented approach for running parallel sessions whose edits must not collide. Claude Code also enforces the isolation: it blocks edits and git commands that target the main checkout from inside a worktree session.

whyWrong.A: Branches in one checkout share one working directory. Switching branches under a running session causes exactly the collisions described.
whyWrong.C: Prompt-level scoping is advisory. Shared files such as configs and lockfiles will still collide, and a single build directory is still shared.
whyWrong.D: Plan mode controls when edits happen, not where. Approved edits from the two sessions still land in the same files.

questions.mindset: Isolate parallel work structurally (separate checkouts), not by asking the agents to stay out of each other's way.

questions.stem: A developer has two tasks for Claude Code today. The first is fixing a misspelled variable name in a single utility file. The second is replacing a hand-rolled session layer with OAuth, which touches about 40 files, and the team has not yet agreed on the approach. The developer wants a good result on both without wasting time. Which workflow is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Use plan mode for both tasks, so that every change follows the same review-before-edit process.
Use direct execution for both tasks, but give Claude a very detailed prompt for the OAuth change listing every file to touch.
Make the rename directly, and use plan mode to explore and agree on an approach for the OAuth change before any edits.
Make the rename directly, and run the OAuth change in auto mode so the background classifier catches risky edits.

questions.explanation: Planning pays off when the approach is uncertain, the change spans many files, or the code is unfamiliar. The docs' rule of thumb: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. So the rename should be done **directly**, and the OAuth migration should go through **explore → plan → approve → implement** in plan mode, where Claude reads and proposes but does not edit source until the plan is approved.

whyWrong.A: Planning a one-line rename is pure overhead. The docs specifically recommend direct execution for small tasks with a clear scope.
whyWrong.B: The team has not agreed on an approach, so a file list cannot be written yet. Exploration and planning are exactly what this task is missing.
whyWrong.D: Auto mode is a permission mechanism that screens risky actions. It does not settle which architecture to use, so it can carry out the wrong design without any prompts.

questions.mindset: Match process weight to uncertainty: plan when the approach is open, act directly when the diff is obvious.

questions.stem: A CI pipeline uses claude -p to implement small fixes, then calls claude -p --continue in the same job to review the change before a pull request opens. The review almost never finds problems, yet human reviewers keep catching edge-case bugs. Also, each time a developer pushes a new commit, the review step posts the same comments again. Which TWO changes BEST address these problems? Choose TWO.

options.text: Run the review as a fresh invocation that does not resume the authoring session, giving it only the diff and review criteria.
Increase --max-turns and the thinking budget on the review step so the reviewer has more room to examine every changed file thoroughly.
Pass the previous review's findings into the review prompt and ask it to report only issues that are new or still unresolved.
Have the authoring session rate its confidence in each finding and post only findings rated above a fixed threshold.
Switch the review step to a larger model while keeping --continue so it still has the implementation context.

questions.explanation: A session that wrote the code keeps its own reasoning and tends to agree with it. A **fresh, independent reviewer** sees only the diff and criteria, so it judges the result on its own terms (the writer/reviewer pattern). The duplicate comments come from re-reviewing without memory of earlier runs, so **feeding prior findings in** and asking for only new or unresolved issues fixes that.

whyWrong.B: More turns do not remove the self-review bias. The reviewer still reasons from the author's context.
whyWrong.D: Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated, and it does nothing about the bias or the duplicate comments.
whyWrong.E: A larger model that still reuses the author's context has the same confirmation bias. Model size is not the root cause here.

questions.mindset: Never let the author grade its own work; give the reviewer fresh context plus memory of what was already reported.

questions.stem: A CI step runs claude -p to triage failing tests, and a dashboard reads the output. Today a regex parses Claude's prose for a severity, a file path, and a suggested owner, and it breaks whenever the wording changes. The team wants the most reliable machine-readable result with minimal changes to the pipeline. What should they do?

options.text: Add "Respond only with JSON" to the prompt along with three example responses, and parse stdout with a JSON parser.
Run with --output-format json and a --json-schema describing the three fields, then read the structured_output field.
Switch to --output-format stream-json, join the text deltas, and run the existing regex on the joined text.
Add a second claude -p call that converts the first call's prose into JSON before the dashboard reads it.

questions.explanation: `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` makes Claude Code validate the result against the schema and return it in the `structured_output` field of the JSON response. It is a single-flag change that replaces fragile text parsing with a schema-checked contract.

whyWrong.A: Prompt instructions and examples improve compliance, but they do not guarantee it. Stray text or a changed shape will still break the parser at some point.
whyWrong.C: Streaming changes how the output arrives, not what it contains. The regex is just as fragile.
whyWrong.D: A second unvalidated model call adds latency and cost, and it is still free-form output. It hides the problem instead of enforcing a schema.

questions.mindset: When code consumes model output, enforce a schema at the boundary; don't negotiate format in the prompt.

questions.stem: Developers on a payments team ask Claude Code for a security review of their changes several times a week. Two problems keep coming up. The review reads dozens of files and fills the main conversation, so the implementation work that follows suffers. And the reviewer sometimes edits code "helpfully" instead of only reporting findings. The team wants one reusable, shared setup that solves both problems. What should they set up?

options.text: A section in the project CLAUDE.md that explains how to run a security review, including a rule that reviews must never modify files.
A project skill holding the review checklist that runs in the main conversation, with a line telling Claude not to edit files during a review.
A team convention of running every review in plan mode in the main session, so Claude cannot edit source until a plan is approved.
A project subagent in .claude/agents/ with a review-focused system prompt and a tools list limited to Read, Grep and Glob, committed to git.

questions.explanation: A **subagent** runs in its own context window and returns only its findings, so the dozens of file reads never enter the main conversation. Its `tools` field is an allowlist: a subagent limited to `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` has no tool that can edit or write files, so the "helpful fix" cannot happen. That is a structural limit, not a request. Project subagents live in `.claude/agents/` and are meant to be checked into version control so the whole team uses the same reviewer.

whyWrong.A: CLAUDE.md is advisory context loaded in every session. It does not stop edits, and the review still runs in the main conversation and fills it.
whyWrong.B: Running in the main conversation leaves the context problem in place, and a line asking Claude not to edit is still only an instruction.
whyWrong.C: Plan mode does block source edits, but the review still reads every file into the main conversation, so only one of the two problems is solved.

questions.mindset: Give a recurring side task its own context and only the tools it needs.

questions.stem: Developers start long unattended Claude Code sessions to fix flaky tests. Claude often reports "done" while the suite is still failing, and someone notices hours later. The team wants a deterministic gate, enforced by Claude Code rather than by the model's own judgment, that stops a turn from ending while the test suite is failing. What is the MOST effective control?

options.text: Add a Stop hook that runs the test suite and blocks the stop, feeding the failures back to Claude, while any test fails.
Add a CLAUDE.md rule requiring Claude to run the full test suite and confirm it passes before saying it is finished.
Add a PostToolUse hook that runs the full suite after every edit and exits with code 2 when tests fail.
End every prompt by asking Claude to review its own work and confirm the tests pass before it ends the session.

questions.explanation: A **Stop hook** runs when Claude tries to end its turn. Exiting 2 (or returning `decision: "block"`) prevents the stop, and the reason is fed back so Claude keeps working. The best-practices guide names this as the deterministic gate that lets an unattended run finish correctly. Know the loop protection too: the hook input carries `stop_hook_active`, and Claude Code applies an 8-consecutive-continuation cap (adjustable with `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP`) so a condition that never resolves cannot loop forever.

whyWrong.B: This is advisory. It is the instruction that is already being skipped, just written more strongly.
whyWrong.C: PostToolUse fires after each edit and cannot stop Claude from ending the turn. Running the full suite after every edit also wastes time and money.
whyWrong.D: Self-confirmation is not verification. A model that already believes it is done tends to confirm it.

questions.mindset: Close the verification loop with a check that gates completion, not a request to self-check.

questions.stem: An organization must migrate roughly 2,000 Python modules to a new internal logging API. Each module can be converted on its own, and the existing unit tests confirm each conversion. The work will run unattended overnight. Which approach is MOST effective?

options.text: Open one interactive session in plan mode, approve a detailed migration plan, and let Claude convert all 2,000 modules in that one conversation.
Have Claude write the file list, script a claude -p call per file with scoped --allowedTools, tune the prompt on a few files, then run all.
Script a claude -p call per file in bypassPermissions mode so nothing ever prompts, then triage whatever failed the next morning.
Send every module's source to the Message Batches API for the discount, then apply the returned code with a script.

questions.explanation: The documented fan-out pattern is to generate a task list, loop `claude -p` over it with `--allowedTools` scoped to what the job needs (for example `Edit,Bash(git commit *)`), and **test on 2–3 files first**, refining the prompt before running the full set. Each call has its own clean context and can run the tests, and the scoped tools keep the unattended run safe.

whyWrong.A: Two thousand files in one conversation will fill the context window many times over, and quality degrades as it fills. Plan mode does not change that.
whyWrong.C: bypassPermissions is meant for isolated containers and VMs. It removes the safety net, and skipping the pilot on a few files means a flawed prompt is repeated 2,000 times.
whyWrong.D: A batch request is a one-shot completion with no agentic loop, so Claude cannot run the tests or iterate. Blindly applying the returned code puts verification back on people.

questions.mindset: Scale by fan-out with least-privilege tools, and pilot before running the full set.

questions.stem: A developer has used one Claude Code session all morning: first a CSS fix, then questions about the CI config, and now a cache-invalidation bug in the API. Claude has gotten the cache fix wrong three times. Each time the developer corrects it, and the latest attempt brings back an approach the developer had already rejected. Which TWO actions are MOST likely to produce a correct fix? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep correcting Claude in the same session, since each correction adds information that the next attempt can build on.
Run /clear and restart with a more specific prompt that states what was tried, why it failed, and the constraints learned so far.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the whole morning's history and every correction fit comfortably.
Add an IMPORTANT note to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude never to repeat approaches that were rejected earlier.
Have Claude first write a failing test that reproduces the cache bug, then fix the code and rerun the test until it passes.

questions.explanation: The session shows two documented failure patterns: the **kitchen-sink session** (unrelated tasks in one context) and **correcting over and over** (the context fills with failed approaches). The documented fix is to run `/clear` after two failed corrections and start again with a better prompt that includes what you learned, because a clean session with a better prompt almost always beats a long one full of corrections. Separately, giving Claude a **check it can run**, such as a failing test that reproduces the bug, lets it iterate until the check passes instead of stopping when the fix only looks done.

whyWrong.A: More corrections add more failed attempts to the context. That noise is why the rejected approach keeps coming back.
whyWrong.C: The problem is irrelevant and failed content in the context, not a lack of space. A bigger window keeps all of that noise, and performance still degrades as the context fills.
whyWrong.D: CLAUDE.md loads in every session, so it should hold only broadly applicable rules. A vague, session-specific note does not belong there and does not remove the polluted context.

questions.mindset: When a session goes sideways, reset the context with what you learned and give Claude a check it can run.
